Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Notepad++ Plugin Delivers MATCHBOIL.V2 in UAC-0099 Attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    category: file_access
    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine

    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dolphin X C2 beacon to thedolphinx.top / backend.thedolphinx.top build backend
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single process mass-harvesting browser, wallet & password-manager credential stores (Dolphin X sweep) · [LLM] Single process harvesting developer & cloud secrets (.env, SSH keys, AWS/GCP/kube configs) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Dolphin X C2 beacon to thedolphinx.top / backend.thedolphinx.top build backend AICommand & Control High
Hunts host connections and DNS resolutions to the Dolphin X operator infrastructure (thedolphinx.top, backend.thedolphinx.top — build/exfil backend on :8443) and connections originating from the known Dolphin X sample hash. High-fidelity because the domains and backend port are named and corroborated by multiple vendor write-ups. Rationale: Anchored on the named C2 domains thedolphinx.top / backend.thedolphinx.top and the build-backend port 8443 (per Varonis + The Register), plus the article's sample SHA256 as an initiating-process pivot. Corroborated by four independent second sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/ • https://www.technadu.com/dolphin-x-new-windows-stealer-uses-ai-to-rank-which-victims-are-worth-robbing/631754/ • https://gbhackers.com/windows-stealer-uses-ai-profiling/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / TI analyst intentionally sandboxing or resolving the IOC domain from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel feed connector or URL-scanning appliance proactively resolving newly-reported malicious domains
  • Web proxy or DNS sinkhole logging the domain as it blocks it (source is the security tool, not a victim)
  • Unrelated legitimate service coincidentally hosted on :8443 (filter requires the thedolphinx substring to avoid this)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox01","ti-scanner01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 making the connection; if it is not a browser/security tool and matches the sample hash, treat as confirmed. Pull the full DeviceNetworkEvents timeline for that host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block thedolphinx.top and backend.thedolphinx.top at DNS/proxy/firewall, and force-reset credentials for every account used on that machine (browsers, cloud CLIs, SSH). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process across all hosts, search DeviceFileEvents for the credential-store sweep (see companion UCs), and query for any other host resolving the domains in the last 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "thedolphinx.top"
    or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "726e7fe23560fe03ea36163d5f510b494f41a78bf811c92ff219f64b4bfe2be0"
| extend BackendPort8443 = (RemotePort == 8443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, BackendPort8443
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "thedolphinx.top"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Detail=QueryTypeName),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has "thedolphinx.top" or RequestURL has "thedolphinx.top" or (DestinationPort == 8443 and DestinationHostName has "thedolphinx")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Detail=tostring(DestinationPort))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Single process mass-harvesting browser, wallet & password-manager credential stores (Dolphin X sweep) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects one non-machine-account process reading four or more distinct credential stores (Chromium/Gecko Login Data, wallet extension settings, desktop wallet keystores, KeePass vaults) within a 5-minute window — the Dolphin X stealer sweep across 9 browsers, 100+ wallet extensions, 65 desktop wallets and 10 password managers. Includes the known sample SHA256 as a booster. Rationale: Built from the article's explicit collection scope (9 browsers, 100+ wallet extensions, 65 desktop wallets, 10 password managers) expressed as a same-process fan-out across distinct credential file types in a tight window — the behaviour that distinguishes a stealer sweep from normal browser use. Sample SHA256 added as a high-confidence override. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/ • https://gbhackers.com/windows-stealer-uses-ai-profiling/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1555.005 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup / migration agents (e.g. profile-sync, browser-import tools) reading multiple browser profile files at once
  • Enterprise password-manager clients or browser-sync services touching vaults and Login Data
  • Antivirus / EDR full-disk scans opening credential SQLite files during a scheduled scan
  • Browser itself updating multiple profile stores after an upgrade
  • Forensic / DLP agents inventorying credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mbamservice.exe","backup.exe","veeam.agent.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessFileName, folder path and SHA256 — a signed browser/backup tool is likely benign; an unsigned binary in %TEMP%/%APPDATA% or one matching the sample hash is malicious. Confirm the process also beaconed to thedolphinx.top. 2) Contain: isolate the host and reset all browser-saved, wallet, and password-manager credentials plus any crypto seed phrases; assume full compromise of stored secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process SHA256 org-wide, check the developer-secret harvest UC for .env/.ssh/.aws access by the same process, and review outbound uploads to backend.thedolphinx.top.
let window = 5m;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| extend LowerPath = tolower(FolderPath), LowerName = tolower(FileName)
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data For Account","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data"))
    or (LowerPath has @"\local extension settings\")
    or (LowerName endswith ".kdbx")
    or (LowerPath has @"\ethereum\keystore")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(FileName), Stores = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where DistinctStores >= 4 or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "726e7fe23560fe03ea36163d5f510b494f41a78bf811c92ff219f64b4bfe2be0"
| order by FirstSeen desc
let window = 5m;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| extend LowerPath = tolower(TargetFilePath), LowerName = tolower(TargetFileName)
| where (TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data"))
    or (LowerPath has @"\local extension settings\")
    or (LowerName endswith ".kdbx")
    or (LowerPath has @"\ethereum\keystore")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(TargetFileName), Stores = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where DistinctStores >= 4
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Login Data* OR *\\key4.db* OR *\\logins.json* OR *\\cookies.sqlite* OR *\\Web Data* OR *\\Local Extension Settings\\* OR *.kdbx OR *\\ethereum\\keystore*)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/
| TargetFileName=/(\\Login Data|\\key4\.db|\\logins\.json|\\cookies\.sqlite|\\Web Data|\\Local Extension Settings\\|\.kdbx$|\\ethereum\\keystore)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctStores))
| DistinctStores >= 4

Single process harvesting developer & cloud secrets (.env, SSH keys, AWS/GCP/kube configs) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects one non-machine-account process reading three or more distinct developer/cloud secret types (.env files, ~/.ssh private keys, .aws/credentials, gcloud config, .kube/config) within a 10-minute window — the Dolphin X developer/DevOps credential-collection capability that sets it apart from a commodity browser stealer. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's stated developer-secret theft (.env files, SSH keys, cloud access tokens, cloud CLI configs across 30+ cloud CLI tools) as a same-process multi-secret-type access burst — the DevOps-targeting angle that multiple sources call out as Dolphin X's distinguishing collection behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/ • https://www.technadu.com/dolphin-x-new-windows-stealer-uses-ai-to-rank-which-victims-are-worth-robbing/631754/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1528 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a legit build/deploy that reads .env, ~/.ssh and cloud CLI configs (CI runners, terraform, kubectl, aws-cli sessions)
  • IDE / editor (VS Code) indexing a workspace containing .env and config files
  • Backup or endpoint-DLP agent scanning home directories
  • Secret-scanning security tools (gitleaks, trufflehog) walking dev machines
  • Configuration-management agent (Ansible/Chef) reading credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","terraform.exe","aws.exe","kubectl.exe","gcloud.exe","git.exe","python.exe","node.exe","ssh.exe","gitleaks.exe","trufflehog.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the InitiatingProcess is a known dev tool (code.exe, terraform.exe, aws.exe, kubectl.exe, git.exe) — those are usually benign; an unsigned binary in %TEMP%/%APPDATA%, or one matching the sample hash / beaconing to thedolphinx.top, is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host and immediately rotate every exposed secret — SSH keys, AWS/GCP access keys, kube tokens, and any credentials in the read .env files — then review cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/GCP audit) for use of those keys from unfamiliar IPs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process SHA256 org-wide and correlate with the browser/wallet sweep UC and outbound uploads to backend.thedolphinx.top:8443.
let window = 10m;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| extend LowerPath = tolower(FolderPath), LowerName = tolower(FileName)
| where (LowerName == ".env" or LowerName startswith ".env.")
    or (LowerPath has @"\.ssh" and (LowerName startswith "id_" or LowerName endswith ".pem"))
    or (LowerPath has @"\.aws" and LowerName in~ ("credentials","config"))
    or (LowerPath has @"\gcloud")
    or (LowerPath has @"\.kube" and LowerName == "config")
| summarize DistinctSecretPaths = dcount(FolderPath), Secrets = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where DistinctSecretPaths >= 3 or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "726e7fe23560fe03ea36163d5f510b494f41a78bf811c92ff219f64b4bfe2be0"
| order by FirstSeen desc
let window = 10m;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| extend LowerPath = tolower(TargetFilePath), LowerName = tolower(TargetFileName)
| where (LowerName == ".env" or LowerName startswith ".env.")
    or (LowerPath has @"\.ssh" and (LowerName startswith "id_" or LowerName endswith ".pem"))

| order by FirstSeen desc

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FakeAgent fake installer: ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe masquerading as jcef_helper.exe · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Claude app promoted by Bing ads pushes SectopRAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SectopRAT libcef.dll side-load via renamed JetBrains jcef_helper (ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe) · [LLM] FakeAgent scheduled-task persistence created by DockerDesktop.exe · [LLM] SectopRAT secondary persistence: sslconf.exe running from EdgeUpdate\Install with tempdir.dll side-load · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] FakeAgent EtherHiding C2 egress from renamed JetBrains/SPSS loaders · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
SectopRAT libcef.dll side-load via renamed JetBrains jcef_helper (ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the FakeAgent execution primitive: a signed JetBrains Chromium helper (jcef_helper.exe) renamed ClaudeDesktop.exe or DockerDesktop.exe loading a tampered, VMProtect-packed libcef.dll that stages SectopRAT. Article-specific because it pins the loader-name/DLL-name pairing and the known malicious DLL hash rather than generic CEF usage. Rationale: Uses the exact loader-name/DLL pairing (ClaudeDesktop.exe|DockerDesktop.exe sideloading libcef.dll) and the Huntress-published malicious libcef.dll SHA256 26bae4d7... — jcef_helper never legitimately runs under those names, so the pairing is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/anthropic-claude-artifacts-download-malware/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's genuine JetBrains IDE loading libcef.dll — excluded here because it runs as jcef_helper.exe from a JetBrains install path, not ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe
  • An internally-built Electron/CEF app coincidentally named DockerDesktop.exe (real Docker Desktop uses 'Docker Desktop.exe' with a space)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
  • EDR image-load telemetry gaps causing the SHA256 branch not to populate on some agent versions
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\JetBrains\", @"\Program Files\JetBrains") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "jcef_helper.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loader path — legitimate jcef_helper lives under a JetBrains product dir; here it will be in Downloads/%TEMP%/user-writable paths and named ClaudeDesktop.exe or DockerDesktop.exe. Pull the libcef.dll hash and compare to 26bae4d7.... 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process tree, quarantine the ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe + libcef.dll + appcfg.dat. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3/UC4 on the same host for the sslconf.exe EdgeUpdate persistence and BSC/C2 egress; sweep the fleet for the DLL hash and the loader names.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "libcef.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ClaudeDesktop.exe","DockerDesktop.exe")
    or SHA256 == "26bae4d7012bf59847ab4036a065419c3d4ca47e020479f55b3b2c6d0d21394a"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Loader = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          LoaderPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          Dll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, DllSHA256 = SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "libcef.dll"
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "26bae4d7012bf59847ab4036a065419c3d4ca47e020479f55b3b2c6d0d21394a"
    or ActingProcessName has_any ("ClaudeDesktop.exe","DockerDesktop.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeAgent fake installer: ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe masquerading as jcef_helper.exe AIDelivery High
Catches the delivered payload at execution: a binary named ClaudeDesktop.exe or DockerDesktop.exe whose PE OriginalFileName is still jcef_helper.exe, or matching the known benign-JetBrains SHA256 the attacker rebundled. Article-specific masquerade signal from the Bing-malvertising fake Claude Desktop download. Rationale: A PE with FileName ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe but embedded OriginalFileName jcef_helper.exe is a definitional name-masquerade; combined with the Huntress benign-bundle SHA256 f8acb8f5... it is high-fidelity and directly ties to the malvertising delivery step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/23/fakeagent-campaign-malicious-claude-artifact-used-to-distribute-sectoprat-to-29-organisations/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A packaging pipeline that renames a bundled CEF helper for a legit internal app without stripping OriginalFileName (rare)
  • Real Docker Desktop — note it ships as 'Docker Desktop.exe' with a space, so it will not match
  • Genuine Anthropic Claude desktop client if it were ever CEF-based and named ClaudeDesktop.exe (verify signer/publisher)
  • Sandbox/AV re-detonation of the archived sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe") or FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the digital signature/publisher and OriginalFileName; confirm the download referrer chain (Bing sponsored → claude.ai artifact → download-app[.]us). 2) Contain: block execution, isolate host, capture the parent browser process and download URL. 3) Hunt: search proxy/DNS for download-app[.]us, downloading-api.it[.]com and the claude.ai artifact path; sweep endpoints for the ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe hash across the org (29 victims reported).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ClaudeDesktop.exe","DockerDesktop.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "jcef_helper.exe"
    or SHA256 == "f8acb8f5cf88b77a4c27d7fd6856aa299bb178e85f9963c2fbd447d818da3ed0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          OriginalName = ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ClaudeDesktop.exe","DockerDesktop.exe")
| where ActingProcessFileOriginalName =~ "jcef_helper.exe"
    or SHA256 =~ "f8acb8f5cf88b77a4c27d7fd6856aa299bb178e85f9963c2fbd447d818da3ed0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessFileOriginalName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeAgent scheduled-task persistence created by DockerDesktop.exe AIInstallation High
Detects the reinfection persistence step: the masqueraded DockerDesktop.exe (or ClaudeDesktop.exe) spawning schtasks.exe /create to register a task that relaunches the loader. Distinct pivot (task-creation process tree) from the DLL side-load and network UCs. Rationale: jcef_helper (the real identity of DockerDesktop.exe) has no business creating scheduled tasks; parent=DockerDesktop.exe/ClaudeDesktop.exe + schtasks /create is a tightly-scoped persistence signal called out verbatim in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Docker Desktop maintenance tasks (uses 'Docker Desktop.exe' with a space and 'com.docker.service', so will not match this exact parent name)
  • An admin script wrapper coincidentally named ClaudeDesktop.exe registering a task
  • EDR misattributing grandparent as parent during rapid process churn
  • Software packaging tools invoking schtasks under a renamed bootstrapper
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks /create command line to recover the task name and the action path (expect it to point back at DockerDesktop.exe/appcfg.dat). 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, remove the referenced binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks on the host and peers pointing to user-writable paths; correlate with UC1 (libcef.dll) and UC4 (sslconf EdgeUpdate persistence) on the same asset.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("DockerDesktop.exe","ClaudeDesktop.exe")
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("DockerDesktop.exe","ClaudeDesktop.exe")
| where ActingProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FakeAgent Scheduled Task Persistence via DockerDesktop.exe
id: 8b3c5d9a-1f2e-4c7b-a4d3-6e5f7a8b9c0d
description: Detects schtasks.exe /create spawned by the masqueraded DockerDesktop.exe/ClaudeDesktop.exe loader (FakeAgent SectopRAT persistence).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-claude-app-promoted-by-bing-ads-pushes-sectoprat-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

      - '\DockerDesktop.exe'
      - '\ClaudeDesktop.exe'

    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\DockerDesktop.exe OR *\dockerdesktop.exe OR *\ClaudeDesktop.exe OR *\claudedesktop.exe) @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/create* OR *\/CREATE*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/\\?(DockerDesktop|ClaudeDesktop)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("/[Cc]reate", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" (Processes.parent_process_name="DockerDesktop.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="ClaudeDesktop.exe") Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" (Processes.parent_process_name="DockerDesktop.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="ClaudeDesktop.exe") Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
SectopRAT secondary persistence: sslconf.exe running from EdgeUpdate\Install with tempdir.dll side-load AIInstallation High
Hunts the second persistence/side-load: an IBM SPSS binary (sslconf.exe) planted at %APPDATA%\Roaming\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\ that side-loads malicious tempdir.dll (GPU anti-VM). The SPSS binary in an Edge-update directory is a strong location-masquerade signal unique to this campaign. Rationale: sslconf.exe is a legitimate IBM SPSS component; its presence under the Edge auto-update install path (%APPDATA%\Roaming\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\) is the exact location-masquerade Huntress documented for the tempdir.dll side-load, giving a very low-FP, campaign-specific hit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine IBM SPSS Statistics installs run sslconf.exe from Program Files\IBM\SPSS, not the EdgeUpdate path — will not match
  • A misconfigured software-deployment tool staging binaries under EdgeUpdate (extremely unusual)
  • Legitimate Microsoft Edge update (edgeupdate.exe/MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe) — different binary name, excluded
  • AV quarantine restoring the file to its original path
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\IBM\SPSS" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\IBM")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm sslconf.exe hash (benign SSLConf fd826215...) and check the sibling tempdir.dll (SHA256 1cd58cfb...) in the same folder — the DLL is the malicious component. 2) Contain: kill the process, remove the EdgeUpdate\Install\ directory contents, isolate host. 3) Hunt: search for tempdir.dll by hash fleet-wide and enumerate any Run keys/scheduled tasks referencing the EdgeUpdate\Install path; correlate to UC1/UC3 on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "sslconf.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "sslconf.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\" or ActingProcessName has @"\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SectopRAT sslconf.exe Persistence from EdgeUpdate Install Directory
id: 4f7e2a10-9b8c-4d5e-8a1f-3c2b1d0e9f8a
description: Detects IBM SPSS sslconf.exe executing from %APPDATA%\Roaming\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install (FakeAgent SectopRAT tempdir.dll side-load persistence).
references:
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\sslconf.exe'
    Image|contains: '\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\sslconf.exe OR *\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\SSLConf.exe OR *\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\Install\SSLCONF.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\sslconf\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\Microsoft\\\\EdgeUpdate\\\\Install\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="sslconf.exe" Processes.process_path="*\\Microsoft\\EdgeUpdate\\Install\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="sslconf.exe" Processes.process_path="*\\Microsoft\\EdgeUpdate\\Install\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
FakeAgent EtherHiding C2 egress from renamed JetBrains/SPSS loaders AICommand & Control Medium
Flags command-and-control from the masqueraded loaders (ClaudeDesktop.exe/DockerDesktop.exe/sslconf.exe) — including the known SectopRAT C2 2.24.131[.]246 and staging domains — where the blockchain-resolved (EtherHiding via BNB Smart Chain) address is dialed. These helper binaries should never make outbound public connections. Rationale: Combines the Huntress-published SectopRAT C2 IP 2.24.131[.]246 and FakeAgent staging domains with a behavioural anchor — jcef_helper/SPSS loaders making ANY public connection — since EtherHiding rotates the resolved C2 and the domains/IP may age out, the process-egress clause keeps the detection durable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • 2.24.131.246 sits in an Akamai/BT-adjacent range; unrelated hosts contacting that IP for CDN content would be noise if matched without the process anchor (KnownIOC='yes' with a non-loader process)
  • A legit internally-named ClaudeDesktop.exe update check reaching a vendor endpoint
  • Proxy/NAT rewriting InitiatingProcess attribution on some sensors
  • Threat-intel feed already blocking the domains, so egress is a failed connection rather than success
Suppression filter
| where not (KnownIOC == "yes" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ClaudeDesktop.exe","DockerDesktop.exe","sslconf.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is one of the renamed loaders and whether the destination is 2.24.131.246 or a staging domain; pull the connection frequency (EtherHiding-resolved C2 tends to beacon). 2) Contain: block the C2 IP/domains at egress, isolate the host, and note the BSC resolver contracts 0xc1907d7be91f95903ad66d775c397302e7dd9228 / 0xe012d0f34cde9b870e9d9ed566ea5f8fd9b92228 for intel enrichment. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts where these loaders made public egress, and check DNS logs for the FakeAgent domains across the estate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ClaudeDesktop.exe","DockerDesktop.exe","sslconf.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| extend KnownIOC = iff(RemoteIP == "2.24.131.246"
        or RemoteUrl has_any ("download-app.us","downloading-api.it.com","5ca8758c-02d0-4a72-89c8-d468b66dda41.com"), "yes","no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, KnownIOC
| order by KnownIOC desc, Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "2.24.131.246"
    or Url has_any ("download-app.us","downloading-api.it.com","5ca8758c-02d0-4a72-89c8-d468b66dda41.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FakeAgent SectopRAT C2 Egress from Masqueraded Loaders
id: 9a1b2c3d-4e5f-4061-8273-5a6b7c8d9e0f
description: Detects outbound connections to SectopRAT C2 2.24.131.246 / FakeAgent staging domains or any public egress from the renamed JetBrains/SPSS loaders.
references:
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1102.001
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_c2:
    DestinationIp: '2.24.131.246'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\ClaudeDesktop.exe'
      - '\DockerDesktop.exe'
      - '\sslconf.exe'
    Initiated: 'true'
  condition: selection_c2 or selection_proc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:2.24.131.246 OR @DestinationHostname:(*download-app.us* OR *downloading-api.it.com* OR *5ca8758c-02d0-4a72-89c8-d468b66dda41.com*) OR @Image:(*\ClaudeDesktop.exe OR *\claudedesktop.exe OR *\DockerDesktop.exe OR *\dockerdesktop.exe OR *\sslconf.exe OR *\SSLConf.exe))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemoteAddressIP4="2.24.131.246" OR ContextImageFileName=/\\(ClaudeDesktop|DockerDesktop|sslconf)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="ClaudeDesktop.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="DockerDesktop.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="sslconf.exe") All_Traffic.dest_is_internal=false by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval known_c2=if(dest=="2.24.131.246","yes","no") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="ClaudeDesktop.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="DockerDesktop.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="sslconf.exe") All_Traffic.dest_is_internal=false by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval known_c2=if(dest=="2.24.131.246","yes","no") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user

Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-23 21 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian state-supported espionage group spent months reading Western mailboxes through a then-unknown flaw in Zimbra's webmail client. The payload goes after the last 90 days of email, the organization's entire email directory, the password saved in the browser and the codes kept for two-factor recovery. Opening the message was enough to start it. The NSA, CISA and partner agencies published

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest · [LLM] Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE) for MFA-less mailbox access · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ZimReaper C2/DNS callout to TA488 Zimbra-themed infrastructure (CVE-2025-66376) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ZimReaper DNS-tunnel exfiltration via long random subdomains of actor domains · [LLM] Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call · [LLM] ZimReaper Global Address List brute-force enumeration (two-character SOAP sweep) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ZimReaper C2/DNS callout to TA488 Zimbra-themed infrastructure (CVE-2025-66376) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS resolution and network connections to the nine TA488/ZimReaper C2 domains and nine C2 IPs used to exfiltrate stolen Zimbra mail, passwords and 2FA scratch codes. Article-specific because it pins the exact adversary infrastructure that Unit 42 (CL-STA-1114) and Proofpoint (TA488) both attributed to the same servers. Rationale: Uses the nine domains and nine IPs that The Hacker News confirmed appear in BOTH Unit 42's and Proofpoint's indicator lists (same infrastructure ties CL-STA-1114 to TA488), so these are second-source-validated IOCs, not single-article claims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://securityaffairs.com/189673/security/russian-apt-targets-ukraine-via-zimbra-xss-flaw-cve-2025-66376.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating a sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform actively resolving IOC domains for feeds
  • Typosquat-lookalike legitimate 'emailanalytics.com' marketing traffic vs the '.com.ua' actor domain — verify exact TLD
  • A defender's own C2 sinkhole or DNS-block-page infrastructure resolving these names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and RemoteUrl != "emailanalytics.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host + initiating process (a browser rendering Zimbra webmail is expected for ZimReaper) and the exact indicator hit; confirm the domain TLD/IP matches the IOC list exactly. 2) Contain: block the domain/IP at DNS and egress, isolate the host, and treat every Zimbra mailbox that host authenticated to as compromised — reset password, kill active sessions, regenerate 2FA scratch codes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the src IP across all DNS logs for the long-random-subdomain exfil pattern, and query /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for CreateAppSpecificPassword('ZimbraWeb') and GetScratchCodesRequest tied to that user.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["analyticemailmeter.com","emailanalytics.com.ua","istc-cloud.com","mailnalysis.com","synacorzimbra.nl","zimbra-metadata.com","zimbrastat.com","zimbrasoft.com.ua","zmailanalytics.com"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["37.120.247.228","64.226.124.190","104.248.134.194","185.86.79.95","193.238.152.66","194.156.103.193","216.252.238.18","216.252.238.64","216.252.238.104"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["analyticemailmeter.com","emailanalytics.com.ua","istc-cloud.com","mailnalysis.com","synacorzimbra.nl","zimbra-metadata.com","zimbrastat.com","zimbrasoft.com.ua","zmailanalytics.com"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["37.120.247.228","64.226.124.190","104.248.134.194","185.86.79.95","193.238.152.66","194.156.103.193","216.252.238.18","216.252.238.64","216.252.238.104"]);
union
 (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (C2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Kind="DNS"),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (C2IPs) | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Indicator=DestinationIP, Kind="Firewall")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*analyticemailmeter.com","*emailanalytics.com.ua","*istc-cloud.com","*mailnalysis.com","*synacorzimbra.nl","*zimbra-metadata.com","*zimbrastat.com","*zimbrasoft.com.ua","*zmailanalytics.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
