ZimReaper DNS-tunnel exfiltration via long random subdomains of actor domains AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioral hunt for the ZimReaper exfiltration channel: the payload encodes stolen CSRF tokens, browser passwords, 2FA scratch codes and mailbox data into many long high-entropy subdomains under actor domains (e.g. js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua). Distinct from the IOC-match UC because it catches NEW subdomains/hosts by shape, not by a fixed list. Rationale: Anchors on the two observed staging/exfil hosts (js-l1wt597cimk / js-26tik3egye4 .i.zimbrasoft.com.ua) which share the pattern of a 12-char random label under the actor's registered domains — the article states exfil is 'over DNS queries' with 'long random subdomain lookups'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-ghostmail-zimbra-xss-russian-apt-ukraine/
ATT&CKT1048.003 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately re-registered actor domain now serving benign parked/CDN content with random-looking hostnames
  • Internal DNS resolver/forwarder aggregating many clients' queries into one ClientIP inflating the distinct count
  • Security scanner probing the domains generating varied subdomain lookups
  • CDN or ESP using genuinely long hashed subdomains under a lookalike domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") and DeviceName !contains "dns"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent domain is one of the actor domains and inspect the subdomain labels for base32/hex encoding rather than dictionary words; identify the initiating browser process and the Zimbra user session. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the parent domain at the resolver, isolate the host, and force credential + 2FA-scratch-code rotation for the affected mailbox. 3) Hunt: decode a sample of the subdomains if possible, and check /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for the preceding GetScratchCodesRequest / CreateAppSpecificPassword calls from the same account to confirm the full ZimReaper chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "zimbrasoft.com.ua" or RemoteUrl endswith "zimbra-metadata.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "zmailanalytics.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "emailanalytics.com.ua"
| extend Leftmost = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".")[0])
| summarize DistinctSubdomains = dcount(RemoteUrl), MaxLabelLen = max(strlen(Leftmost)), SampleHost = any(RemoteUrl), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctSubdomains > 20 or MaxLabelLen >= 12   // ZimReaper encodes stolen data into many long (>=12 char) random subdomains; benign autocomplete/telemetry to one host stays low
| order by DistinctSubdomains desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "zimbrasoft.com.ua" or Name endswith "zimbra-metadata.com" or Name endswith "zmailanalytics.com" or Name endswith "emailanalytics.com.ua"
| extend Leftmost = tostring(split(Name, ".")[0])
| summarize DistinctSubdomains = dcount(Name), MaxLabelLen = max(strlen(Leftmost)), SampleHost = any(Name), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by ClientIP, Computer
| where DistinctSubdomains > 20 or MaxLabelLen >= 12   // high-entropy long-label subdomains = DNS-tunnel exfil
| order by DistinctSubdomains desc
source:windows.sysmon @DestinationHostname:(*.zimbrasoft.com.ua OR *.zimbra-metadata.com OR *.zmailanalytics.com OR *.emailanalytics.com.ua)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/\.(zimbrasoft\.com\.ua|zimbra-metadata\.com|zmailanalytics\.com|emailanalytics\.com\.ua)$/i
| leftmost := splitString(DomainName, by=".", index=0)
| label_len := length(leftmost)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=DomainName, distinct=true, as=distinct_subdomains), max(label_len, as=max_label_len)])
| distinct_subdomains > 20 OR max_label_len >= 12
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(DNS.query) as distinct_subdomains from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*.zimbrasoft.com.ua" OR DNS.query="*.zimbra-metadata.com" OR DNS.query="*.zmailanalytics.com" OR DNS.query="*.emailanalytics.com.ua") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | eval leftmost=mvindex(split(query,"."),0) | eval label_len=len(leftmost) | stats sum(count) as queries dc(query) as distinct_subdomains max(label_len) as max_label_len values(query) as sample by src | where distinct_subdomains > 20 OR max_label_len >= 12
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(DNS.query) as distinct_subdomains from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*.zimbrasoft.com.ua" OR DNS.query="*.zimbra-metadata.com" OR DNS.query="*.zmailanalytics.com" OR DNS.query="*.emailanalytics.com.ua") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | eval leftmost=mvindex(split(query,"."),0) | eval label_len=len(leftmost) | stats sum(count) as queries dc(query) as distinct_subdomains max(label_len) as max_label_len values(query) as sample by src | where distinct_subdomains > 20 OR max_label_len >= 12
Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest AIInstallation High
Alerts on ZimReaper's persistence primitive: a SOAP CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest that mints an app-specific password named ZimbraWeb, which grants IMAP/POP3/SMTP access without 2FA and survives password resets. This is the single highest-fidelity host-side IOC from Proofpoint's and Seqrite's guidance. Rationale: The credential name 'ZimbraWeb' is an exact, attacker-chosen string that Proofpoint says to grep /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for and remove — it is near-zero in normal use, making CreateAppSpecificPassword+ZimbraWeb a very high-fidelity, low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1098 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately naming their own app password 'ZimbraWeb' (rare but possible — verify the source session/IP)
  • Admin bulk-provisioning app passwords during an IMAP client rollout
  • A migration/backup tool that creates app-specific passwords programmatically
  • Penetration-test or purple-team activity replaying the TTP
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full audit.log line — capture the target account, source IP and the session that issued the SOAP call; confirm the app password name is 'ZimbraWeb' (or a close variant). 2) Contain: delete the ZimbraWeb app-specific password immediately, disable IMAP/POP if not needed, reset the account password AND invalidate sessions (note: app passwords survive resets, so deletion is mandatory). 3) Hunt: search audit.log for the same account's GetScratchCodesRequest and zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE changes, and check whether the mailserver later sent further exploit emails (compromised-relay reuse).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "CreateAppSpecificPassword" and SyslogMessage has "ZimbraWeb"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog CreateAppSpecificPassword ZimbraWeb
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "CreateAppSpecificPassword" "ZimbraWeb" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample by host account | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on ZimReaper pulling the account's two-factor recovery (scratch) codes through Zimbra's own GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP API — a call that should be close to absent in normal operation. Stolen scratch codes let the actor re-authenticate even after a password reset and session revocation. Rationale: Proofpoint explicitly recommends alerting on GetScratchCodesRequest because it 'should be close to absent in normal use'; ZimReaper calls it through the platform's own APIs, so any occurrence is a strong credential-access signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1111 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately viewing/regenerating their own 2FA backup codes in account settings
  • Helpdesk-assisted 2FA recovery for a locked-out user
  • Zimbra admin auditing or migrating TOTP settings
  • Security-assessment tooling exercising the SOAP endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the target account and source IP from the audit.log entry; determine whether the request came from the user's normal browser/IP or from a webmail session correlated with an inbound HTML email view. 2) Contain: regenerate (invalidate) the account's 2FA scratch codes, reset the password, and revoke active sessions; check for any co-occurring ZimbraWeb app password and delete it. 3) Hunt: correlate the same account/session against DNS logs for the ZimReaper exfil domains and audit.log for zimbraPrefImapEnabled flips within the same time window.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "GetScratchCodesRequest"
| summarize Count = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by Last desc
source:linux.syslog GetScratchCodesRequest
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "GetScratchCodesRequest" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | rex field=_raw "oip=(?<src_ip>[0-9a-fA-F\.:]+)" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(src_ip) as src_ip by host account | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE) for MFA-less mailbox access AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Seqrite-observed persistence step where ZimReaper flips zimbraPrefImapEnabled to TRUE so the minted app-specific password can reach the mailbox over IMAP without 2FA. Article-specific because it pairs the exact attribute name with the ZimbraWeb app-password TTP. Rationale: Seqrite's January case documented the payload flipping zimbraPrefImapEnabled to TRUE; combined with the ZimbraWeb app password this is the mechanism for durable MFA-less IMAP access, so the literal attribute string is a high-value hunt anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-ghostmail-zimbra-xss-russian-apt-ukraine/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1098 T1556
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User enabling IMAP themselves to add a desktop/mobile mail client
  • Admin bulk-enabling IMAP via a COS (class of service) policy change
  • Mail-migration project turning IMAP on across many accounts
  • Provisioning automation setting mailbox prefs at account creation
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account and whether the change came from an admin console session or a user webmail session; check the timestamp against any inbound HTML email view for that user. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, set zimbraPrefImapEnabled back to FALSE, delete any ZimbraWeb app password, reset credentials and regenerate 2FA scratch codes. 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts with zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE that have no business need for IMAP (per Proofpoint guidance) and cross-check them against the GetScratchCodesRequest and app-password alerts.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "zimbraPrefImapEnabled" and SyslogMessage has "TRUE"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog zimbraPrefImapEnabled TRUE
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "zimbraPrefImapEnabled" "TRUE" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample by host account | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
ZimReaper Global Address List brute-force enumeration (two-character SOAP sweep) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects ZimReaper's directory-harvest step: it brute-forces the Global Address List by querying every two-character combination until the entire directory is returned, producing a burst of GAL search SOAP requests from a single Zimbra session far above normal autocomplete usage. Rationale: The article states the payload 'brute-forces the Global Address List, querying every two-character combination until the whole list comes back' — a volumetric GAL-search pattern that a per-session count threshold on the SearchGalRequest SOAP op surfaces cleanly. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1087.003 T1087
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Large mail-merge or CRM sync tool enumerating the GAL for contact caching
  • A newly onboarded user's client aggressively pre-caching the directory
  • Admin address-book export or bulk-provisioning script
  • A shared-account/kiosk session generating many autocomplete lookups
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the query source is a single user session and inspect whether the search terms iterate systematically through two-character strings (a→az, etc.) rather than real name fragments. 2) Contain: terminate the session, reset the account and rotate 2FA scratch codes; if the account is confirmed compromised, treat the whole GAL as harvested. 3) Hunt: correlate the session with GetScratchCodesRequest / CreateAppSpecificPassword(ZimbraWeb) calls and with outbound DNS to the actor domains within the same window to confirm ZimReaper rather than a benign bulk tool.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "SearchGalRequest"
| summarize GalQueries = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where GalQueries > 100   // two-char enumeration ~ 36^2 (>1200) requests; normal autocomplete rarely exceeds a handful per 10m
| order by GalQueries desc
source:linux.syslog SearchGalRequest
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "SearchGalRequest" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | bin _time span=10m | stats count as gal_queries by _time host account | where gal_queries > 100 | sort - gal_queries
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.120.247.228", "64.226.124.190", "104.248.134.194", "185.86.79.95", "193.238.152.66", "194.156.103.193", "216.252.238.18", "216.252.238.64", "216.252.238.104") or RemoteUrl has_any ("analyticemailmeter.com", "emailanalytics.com.ua", "istc-cloud.com", "mailnalysis.com", "synacorzimbra.nl", "zimbra-metadata.com", "zimbrastat.com", "zimbrasoft.com.ua", "zmailanalytics.com", "js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua")

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:

        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or SHA1 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or MD5 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or SHA1 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or MD5 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData (msaRAT delivery)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Don’t swing at everything
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msiexec executing MSI masquerading as Windows update from ProgramData · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent (CDP abuse) · [LLM] Plain-HTTP over port 443 to msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 · [LLM] Browser contacting msaRAT WebRTC signaling relay (workers.dev Cloudflare Worker) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData (msaRAT delivery) AIDelivery High
Hunts msaRAT's initial delivery step where curl.exe pulls an MSI impersonating a Windows update into C:\ProgramData over plain HTTP. Article-specific because it pairs the curl LOLBin with both a .msi extension and a ProgramData drop path — Talos explicitly flags this exact command shape. Rationale: Uses the exact Talos-described command shape (curl + .msi + ProgramData). Two independent sources (BleepingComputer, The Hacker News) confirm curl.exe pulls the MSI into ProgramData, making this high-fidelity rather than a generic ingress-tool-transfer template. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software packaging/deployment tooling using curl to stage MSI installers in ProgramData
  • IT admin manually downloading a vendor MSI to a ProgramData staging folder
  • RMM/patch-management agents (e.g. Chocolatey, PDQ) that fetch MSIs via curl
  • CI/build agents that pull MSI artifacts into ProgramData for testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pdqdeployrunner.exe","choco.exe","chocolatey.exe","ninite.exe","tacticalrmm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and the source URL/IP; confirm whether the host has legitimate deployment tooling that uses curl, and check the SHA256 of the dropped MSI against Talos IOCs. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the source IP (172.86.126.18) at the firewall, and quarantine the MSI in ProgramData before it is executed by msiexec. 3) Hunt: search the host and peers for subsequent msiexec.exe execution of the ProgramData MSI, chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProgramData"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi" and CommandLine has "ProgramData"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msiexec executing MSI masquerading as Windows update from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Hunts msaRAT's execution step: msiexec launching a curl-dropped MSI from ProgramData whose name impersonates a Windows update/patch, whose install runs a custom action loading a DLL from inside the installer straight into memory. Article-specific via the ProgramData path plus update/patch/KB naming lure. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed masquerade (MSI posing as a Windows update dropped in ProgramData) reported by Talos and echoed by The Hacker News. Legitimate Windows updates never install from ProgramData via a curl-dropped MSI, so the path+name combination is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party app updaters that stage MSIs in a vendor ProgramData subfolder with 'update' in the name
  • Enterprise patch tooling repackaging updates as MSIs staged in ProgramData
  • Driver/firmware update MSIs (e.g. Dell/HP) named with 'update' running from ProgramData
  • Internal software distribution that names MSIs after KB numbers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pdqdeployrunner.exe","choco.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","dellcommandupdate.exe","hpsupportassistant.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the MSI path/name and its SHA256, and identify the parent process — a curl.exe or unknown ProgramData binary parent is a strong TP signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill/quarantine the msiexec chain; snapshot memory since the custom action loads a DLL directly into memory. 3) Hunt: look for the browser being launched with --remote-debugging-port shortly after, connections to 172.86.126.18:443 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, and stage for possible ransomware pre-encryption behavior.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProgramData"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","patch","windows","KB")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "ProgramData" and CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","patch","windows","KB")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Msiexec Running Windows-Update-Themed MSI from ProgramData

Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent (CDP abuse) AICommand & Control High
Hunts msaRAT driving Chrome or Edge over the Chrome DevTools Protocol by starting the browser with a --remote-debugging-port flag, typically spawned by the malicious loader rather than a user shell. This is the core living-off-the-browser C2 setup Talos describes. Rationale: Talos and multiple write-ups (BleepingComputer, Gridinsoft) confirm msaRAT starts a headless browser and drives it via CDP; the --remote-debugging-port flag is the observable that enables CDP. Excluding legit browser/explorer parents removes the bulk of benign automation while keeping the loader-spawned case. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/msarat-chrome-edge-browser-c2/
ATT&CKT1205 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing frameworks (Selenium, Puppeteer, Playwright) launching Chrome with a debug port
  • Developers manually debugging web apps with remote debugging enabled
  • Electron/CEF-based apps that invoke chromium with a debugging port
  • Headless-Chrome PDF/screenshot rendering services spawned by app servers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","selenium.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "playwright"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and its folder path — a parent from ProgramData or an unsigned/unknown binary is a strong TP; check for a co-occurring loopback (127.0.0.1) CDP connection. 2) Contain: isolate the host and terminate the parent loader plus the debug-port browser instance. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host reaching is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev (WebRTC signaling) and Twilio TURN, and look back for the curl→MSI→msiexec delivery chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","code.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\chrome.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Browser Started with Remote Debugging Port by Non-Browser Parent (msaRAT CDP)

Plain-HTTP over port 443 to msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's evasive delivery channel: unencrypted HTTP to the confirmed C2/staging IP 172.86.126.18 on port 443, which slips past firewalls that trust 443 by number without protocol inspection. Anchored on the confirmed network IOC plus the plaintext-on-443 behavior Talos calls out. Rationale: 172.86.126.18:443 is a confirmed IOC (Talos IOC table, echoed by Help Net Security). Talos specifically notes the traffic is plain HTTP on 443 to bypass port-only firewall rules, so pairing the exact IP with port 443 (and HttpConnectionInspected on 443 as the plaintext behavior) is high-confidence and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • If the IP is later reassigned to a benign hosting tenant, unrelated legitimate traffic could hit it
  • Security scanners/threat-intel validation tooling deliberately probing the IOC IP
  • Proxy or gateway appliances logging the connection on behalf of many hosts (source attribution noise)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (curl.exe or a ProgramData binary is a strong TP) and whether the payload on 443 was HTTP rather than TLS. 2) Contain: block 172.86.126.18 org-wide at egress, isolate any host that connected, and preserve the downloaded MSI. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hosts for browser --remote-debugging-port launches and DNS/connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, and sweep the environment for other hosts touching this IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18"
| where RemotePort == 443 or ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" and DestinationPort == 443
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Connection to msaRAT Delivery IP 172.86.126.18 on 443

Browser contacting msaRAT WebRTC signaling relay (workers.dev Cloudflare Worker) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the msaRAT C2 signaling stage where the hijacked Chrome/Edge browser performs SDP offer/answer exchange with the Cloudflare Worker is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev before opening a WebRTC data channel via Twilio TURN. Anchored on the confirmed signaling-relay domain IOC. Rationale: is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev is the confirmed signaling-relay IOC (Talos IOC table, corroborated by Help Net Security/Security Affairs describing SDP exchange with a Cloudflare Worker). A resolution/connection to this exact FQDN is a direct C2 hit; the WebRTC channel itself (Twilio TURN/UDP 3478) is too noisy to detect standalone, so this domain is the reliable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1205
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • If the specific Worker subdomain is sinkholed/reassigned, benign scanner traffic could hit it
  • Threat-intel or DFIR tooling deliberately resolving the IOC domain during validation
  • Web proxy logging the lookup on behalf of many clients, obscuring the true source host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which process resolved/connected to the domain — a browser process (chrome.exe/msedge.exe) driven via CDP is the expected msaRAT pattern. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.ols-img-12.workers.dev (and the exact FQDN) at DNS/egress, isolate the host, and terminate the browser instance carrying the WebRTC channel. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host for --remote-debugging-port browser launches, 127.0.0.1 CDP loopback traffic, connections to 172.86.126.18:443, and the upstream curl→MSI delivery; check for staged ransomware activity.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl)
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query for msaRAT WebRTC Signaling Relay (workers.dev)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UAC-0099 VBS launcher masquerading as PDF (Evernote.zip retriever)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Notepad++ 8.8.3 side-loading NppExport.dll (LunchPoke) from non-standard path · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers abuse Notepad++ plugins to stealthily install malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Scheduled task created from Notepad++/LunchPoke execution context · [LLM] WinRAR extracting updater.rar then BurnyBear (RemoteLibUpdater.exe) / InitTest.dll execution · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] UAC-0099 second-stage / C2 domains contacted (imageurlgenerator, easysend, filemail, cutt.ly) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] BurnyBear resource-exhaustion fallback (rapid process/CPU-RAM burst)
UAC-0099 VBS launcher masquerading as PDF (Evernote.zip retriever) AIDelivery High
Hunts wscript.exe/cscript.exe executing a script that carries a .pdf name/double-extension and then reaches out for the second-stage Evernote.zip archive. This is the UAC-0099 initial-access lure where a VBS is disguised as a PDF document inside the delivered ZIP. Rationale: Article states UAC-0099 'delivers a ZIP archive with a VBS script disguised as a PDF document' that 'retrieves another compressed file named Evernote.zip' — the .pdf-named-script + Evernote.zip strings are article-specific, high-fidelity delivery markers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/notepad-used-in-new-stealthy-attacks-targeting-ukraine • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/cve-2025-56383-the-essential-notepad-guide-for-defenders/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin scripts that open PDFs via WScript.Shell for automated report generation
  • QA/document-conversion tooling that passes .pdf paths to a .vbs helper
  • Legacy line-of-business apps invoking cscript with a PDF output filename
  • Backup/archival scripts referencing .zip and .pdf in the same command line
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and AccountName in~ ("svc-report","svc-batch"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the on-disk script; confirm the .pdf-named file is actually VBScript (check file magic / first bytes) and whether Evernote.zip was fetched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript process tree, and quarantine the delivered ZIP and any randomly-named install directory. 3) Hunt: search for a subsequent Notepad++ 8.8.3 drop, NppExport.dll load, updater.rar, and scheduled-task creation on the same host and across peers who received the same lure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".pdf"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs", "Evernote.zip", ".zip")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".pdf"
| where CommandLine has_any (".vbs","Evernote.zip",".zip")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: VBS Script Executed With PDF Name (UAC-0099 Notepad++ Lure)
id: 6f3c2a90-8b41-4e2a-9c77-2d51a0e1b7f4
description: wscript/cscript running a script that carries a .pdf name/extension, matching UAC-0099 VBS-disguised-as-PDF delivery.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
  - https://www.scworld.com/brief/notepad-used-in-new-stealthy-attacks-targeting-ukraine
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1566.001
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '.pdf'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @CommandLine:(*.pdf* AND (*.vbs* OR *Evernote.zip* OR *.zip*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i | regex("(?i)\.pdf", field=CommandLine) | regex("(?i)(\.vbs|Evernote\.zip|\.zip)", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") Processes.process="*.pdf*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)\.pdf") AND (match(process, "(?i)\.vbs") OR match(parent_process_name, "(?i)(explorer|7zFM|winrar|winzip)\.exe")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") Processes.process="*.pdf*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)\.pdf") AND (match(process, "(?i)\.vbs") OR match(parent_process_name, "(?i)(explorer|7zFM|winrar|winzip)\.exe")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Notepad++ 8.8.3 side-loading NppExport.dll (LunchPoke) from non-standard path AIExploitation High
Detects notepad++.exe loading or a process dropping NppExport.dll outside the legitimate Notepad++ plugins directory — the LunchPoke plugin side-load abusing CVE-2025-56383. Article-specific because it pins the exact binary name and the randomly-named install directory behaviour. Rationale: Article names the exact malicious plugin 'NppExport.dll' (LunchPoke) loaded via Notepad++'s plugin mechanism into a 'randomly named directory'; loading that DLL from any path other than the real plugins folder is the CVE-2025-56383 side-load signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/cve-2025-56383-the-essential-notepad-guide-for-defenders/ • https://gbhackers.com/notepad-dll-hijack-flaw/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/USB Notepad++ builds where the plugins folder path differs from Program Files
  • User-compiled NppExport.dll (JetNpp fork) in a custom plugins location
  • Software-deployment tools staging Notepad++ into a temp folder before install
  • Developers testing plugins from a build output directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: get the DLL SHA256 and compare against the legitimate NppExport.dll hash; note the parent directory (random name = strong indicator). 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate notepad++.exe, quarantine the DLL and the whole install directory including updater.rar and the bundled WinRAR. 3) Hunt: pivot to scheduled-task creation, RemoteLibUpdater.exe/InitTest.dll extraction, and outbound connections to cdn.imageurlgenerator.com / easysend.co from this host.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NppExport.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "notepad++.exe"
| where FolderPath !contains @"\Notepad++\plugins\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "NppExport.dll"
| where TargetFilePath !contains @"\Notepad++\plugins\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256

Scheduled task created from Notepad++/LunchPoke execution context AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when a scheduled task is created by the Notepad++ process lineage or references non-standard loader paths (RemoteLibUpdater.exe). LunchPoke and the downstream MatchBoil V2 loader each create a scheduled task for persistence, which is anomalous for a text editor. Rationale: Article states LunchPoke 'creates a scheduled task on Windows' and the MatchBoil V2 loader 'creates another scheduled task' — a scheduled task parented by notepad++.exe/rundll32 or referencing the named loader RemoteLibUpdater.exe is high-fidelity persistence for this chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/notepad-used-in-new-stealthy-attacks-targeting-ukraine
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters registering tasks from a user-writable folder
  • IT automation (SCCM/Intune) creating tasks under a service account
  • Developer tooling that shells out to schtasks.exe during a build
  • Portable app launchers that self-register update tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: export the task XML — inspect the Action's executable path and trigger; a task pointing at a temp/random dir or RemoteLibUpdater.exe is malicious. 2) Contain: disable and delete the task, isolate the host, and kill any running RemoteLibUpdater.exe/BurnyBear process. 3) Hunt: look for a second scheduled task created by the loader, C2 config updates, and WinRAR extraction of downloaded payloads on the same host.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("notepad++.exe","rundll32.exe","RemoteLibUpdater.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "notepad++.exe" or AdditionalFields has "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698
| extend TaskContent = tostring(parse_xml(EventData))
| where TaskContent has_any ("RemoteLibUpdater.exe","notepad++","NppExport","InitTest.dll") or SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where TaskContent has_any ("RemoteLibUpdater.exe","\\Temp\\","AppData\\Local\\Temp")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TaskContent
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @ParentImage:(*\notepad++.exe OR *\Notepad++.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\RunDll32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i | ParentBaseFileName=/(notepad\+\+|rundll32)\.exe$/i OR regex("(?i)RemoteLibUpdater\.exe", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("notepad++.exe","rundll32.exe") OR Processes.process="*RemoteLibUpdater.exe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

WinRAR extracting updater.rar then BurnyBear (RemoteLibUpdater.exe) / InitTest.dll execution AIInstallation High
Detects the legitimate bundled WinRAR extracting the password-protected updater.rar and the subsequent execution of RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BurnyBear loader) which loads InitTest.dll (MatchBoil V2). Named binaries make this a precise, article-specific alert. Rationale: Article names the password-protected 'updater.rar', the legit WinRAR that extracts it, 'RemoteLibUpdater.exe' (BurnyBear) and 'InitTest.dll' (MatchBoil V2) — these exact strings are precise, low-FP execution markers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/notepad-used-in-new-stealthy-attacks-targeting-ukraine
ATT&CKT1105 T1140 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally named RemoteLibUpdater.exe (rare)
  • Admins extracting an unrelated archive named updater.rar
  • Software packagers using WinRAR CLI in build pipelines
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a monitored lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture SHA256 of RemoteLibUpdater.exe and InitTest.dll and check the parent — extraction from a scheduled task or temp dir confirms the chain. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill RemoteLibUpdater.exe and any child processes, quarantine updater.rar and the extracted binaries. 3) Hunt: pull the loader's C2 config, check DeviceNetworkEvents for cdn.imageurlgenerator.com/easysend.co/filemail.com, and look for the resource-exhaustion fallback if execution failed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "updater.rar")
    or FileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "InitTest.dll"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe") and CommandLine has "updater.rar")
    or NewProcessName has "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
    or CommandLine has "InitTest.dll"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: BurnyBear Loader Or updater.rar Extraction (UAC-0099)
id: c4e5f6a7-8b9c-4d10-b2e3-4f5a6b7c8d91
description: WinRAR extracting updater.rar or execution of RemoteLibUpdater.exe/InitTest.dll from the UAC-0099 Notepad++ chain.
references:
