BurnyBear resource-exhaustion fallback (rapid process/CPU-RAM burst) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the BurnyBear fallback that triggers a RAM/CPU resource-exhaustion attack when RemoteLibUpdater.exe fails to launch, surfacing as a burst of child processes from a temp/scheduled-task parent on a single host. Article-specific because it ties the burst to the failed loader launch. Rationale: Article describes BurnyBear's 'fallback mechanism in case launching RemoteLibUpdater.exe fails, triggering a resource exhaustion attack targeting the host's RAM and CPU' — a burst of child processes from the loader/temp context on one host approximates the fork-bomb-style exhaustion. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/notepad-used-in-new-stealthy-attacks-targeting-ukraine
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build/compile jobs that legitimately fork many short-lived cmd.exe children
  • Antivirus/EDR full scans spawning worker processes in bursts
  • Batch-processing scripts iterating over many files with per-file cmd invocations
  • Software installers extracting and launching many helpers from Temp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the burst parent is RemoteLibUpdater.exe or an unsigned binary in Temp, and correlate with a preceding failed loader launch and sustained high CPU/RAM. 2) Contain: isolate the host and terminate the parent process tree to halt the exhaustion loop. 3) Hunt: verify whether the primary loader chain (updater.rar extraction, scheduled task) succeeded elsewhere and confirm C2 reachability on peers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("RemoteLibUpdater.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp")
| summarize ChildCount = count(), Sample = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where ChildCount > 50
| order by ChildCount desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("RemoteLibUpdater.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe")
| summarize ChildCount = count(), Sample = any(NewProcessName) by Computer, ParentProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where ChildCount > 50
| order by ChildCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\RemoteLibUpdater.exe OR *\remotelibupdater.exe OR *\cmd.exe OR *\rundll32.exe) @ParentImage:(*\Temp\* OR *\temp\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(RemoteLibUpdater|cmd|rundll32)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, RawProcessId], function=count()) | count > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("RemoteLibUpdater.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_id _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count > 50 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("RemoteLibUpdater.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_id _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count > 50 | sort - count
UAC-0099 second-stage / C2 domains contacted (imageurlgenerator, easysend, filemail, cutt.ly) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the delivery/C2 infrastructure used in this campaign (cdn.imageurlgenerator.com, easysend.co, filemail.com, cutt.ly) especially when initiated by scripting hosts or the loader. Article/IOC-specific network pivot for the retrieval of Evernote.zip and C2. Rationale: cdn.imageurlgenerator.com, easysend.co, filemail.com and cutt.ly are the pre-extracted campaign domains; scoping to script hosts/loader/temp-dir initiators cuts the noise from legit filemail.com/cutt.ly usage. Note: these IOCs are currently only sourced from the CERT-UA/BleepingComputer reporting, so treat lower-fidelity domains (filemail.com, cutt.ly) as hunting-only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/notepad-used-in-new-stealthy-attacks-targeting-ukraine
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of cutt.ly link shortener in marketing/comms
  • filemail.com used for large-file transfer by business users
  • Security tooling sandbox detonations resolving the domains
  • Threat-intel enrichment services pre-resolving IOC domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a script host, notepad++.exe, or RemoteLibUpdater.exe reaching these domains is far more suspicious than a browser. 2) Contain: block the domains at proxy/DNS, isolate hosts where a non-browser process made the connection. 3) Hunt: on flagged hosts pivot to the full chain (VBS-as-PDF, NppExport.dll load, updater.rar extraction, scheduled tasks) and pull any downloaded payloads from filemail.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("cdn.imageurlgenerator.com","easysend.co","filemail.com","cutt.ly")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","notepad++.exe","RemoteLibUpdater.exe","rundll32.exe","winrar.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Temp\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("cdn.imageurlgenerator.com","easysend.co","filemail.com","cutt.ly")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

npm postinstall dropper spawns osascript (AMOS macOS stealer via @copilot-mcp/apex) AIInstallation High
Hunts a Node/npm process tree spawning osascript on macOS, the exact second-stage behaviour of the @copilot-mcp/apex and @apexfdn/apex droppers that decrypt and run an AMOS-family AppleScript payload. Legitimate npm installs almost never spawn osascript, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated chain (npm install/npx @copilot-mcp/apex -> osascript AppleScript payload). Corroborated by Microsoft and SOC Prime macOS-stealer write-ups that flag node->osascript as the AMOS delivery signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/macos-stealers-observed-what-defenders-should-watch-for/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm package that uses osascript to prompt for permissions during postinstall (rare, e.g. some GUI-integration tooling)
  • Developer manually testing an AppleScript build step from a Node script
  • Electron/Node tooling that shells out to osascript to display native macOS notifications
  • Homebrew Node formula post-install scripts invoking osascript for UI
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","npx","@copilot-mcp/apex","@apexfdn/apex") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("decrypt","base64","do shell script","curl","osalogging")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full osascript command line and the initiating npm/npx command; look for base64, gunzip, curl, JXA, or a decrypt routine in the AppleScript body and check for a package name matching @copilot-mcp/apex or @apexfdn/apex. 2) Contain: isolate the macOS host, kill the osascript/node chain, and revoke any AWS/Kubernetes/SSH creds and browser/crypto-wallet secrets that were on-disk (this stealer harvests them). 3) Hunt: search the same host and package registry usage across the fleet for /tmp/osalogging.zip and LaunchAgents polling a C2, and audit which developers ran that package.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "osascript"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","node.js") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npx ","postinstall","@copilot-mcp/apex","@apexfdn/apex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "osascript"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","node.js") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npx ","postinstall","@copilot-mcp/apex","@apexfdn/apex")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AMOS stealer exfil staging /tmp/osalogging.zip + LaunchAgent C2 persistence (macOS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the AMOS stealer's fixed exfil archive /tmp/osalogging.zip and/or a LaunchAgent plist written alongside osascript/curl activity that polls the C2 every 60 seconds. These are hardcoded artefacts of the @copilot-mcp/apex payload, giving a near-zero-FP alert. Rationale: Uses two fixed article strings: the /tmp/osalogging.zip staging archive and the LaunchAgent that polls C2 every 60s. The zip path is a literal, near-unique IOC; the LaunchAgent+osascript pairing is corroborated by Microsoft/SOC Prime AMOS persistence analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/active-threats/macos-stealers-observed-what-defenders-should-watch-for/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1543.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or backup tool coincidentally naming a zip 'osalogging.zip' (extremely unlikely)
  • Legitimate app writing a LaunchAgent that shells out to curl for update checks
  • Corporate MDM deploying a LaunchAgent for telemetry (whitelist the MDM signing process)
  • Security tooling itself staging archives in /tmp during testing
Suppression filter
| where FileName =~ "osalogging.zip" or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "osascript" and FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (should be osascript or a Node-descended shell); pull the LaunchAgent plist and read its ProgramArguments for the C2 URL and 60s polling loop. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the LaunchAgent and quarantine the payload, and force-rotate every credential class the stealer targets (browser, 20+ crypto wallets, SSH, AWS, Kubernetes, login Keychain, Telegram). 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 host from the plist across DNS/proxy logs, and sweep for node->osascript execution (see companion UC) to find the initial dropper.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osalogging.zip")
    or (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and ActionType == "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("osascript","curl","/tmp/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeAgent: ClaudeDesktop.exe execution + tampered libcef.dll side-load (SectopRAT) AIDelivery High
Hunts the FakeAgent malvertising payload — a fake ClaudeDesktop.exe downloaded from an attacker site (via a Claude.ai artifact redirect) that runs a renamed signed JetBrains binary to side-load a tampered libcef.dll carrying SectopRAT. Targets both the named lure binary and the DLL-sideload-from-staging-dir behaviour. Rationale: ClaudeDesktop.exe is the article's named lure binary (the genuine app ships as Claude.exe). Huntress corroboration adds the tampered libcef.dll side-load loaded from a user-writable staging dir, which the DeviceImageLoadEvents leg catches even if the lure binary is renamed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/anthropic-claude-artifacts-download-malware/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1204.002 T1583.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Claude desktop app (ships as Claude.exe, not ClaudeDesktop.exe) — name mismatch keeps FP low
  • Legitimate CEF/Electron apps (Spotify, Steam, portable browsers) loading libcef.dll from install dirs — excluded by the staging-dir path filter
  • A portable/dev build of a real app run from Downloads that legitimately carries libcef.dll
  • Internal software repackaging that stages CEF apps in Temp during MSI extraction
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and Signal == "libcef.dll side-load from staging dir")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the ClaudeDesktop.exe path/hash against the genuine Claude.exe; inspect the process that loaded libcef.dll for a valid JetBrains signature but an out-of-place folder (Downloads/Temp), and check for VMProtect packing and a GPU/graphics-hardware check (anti-VM). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, quarantine the ClaudeDesktop.exe bundle and tampered libcef.dll, and block the attacker download domain. 3) Hunt: pivot to the companion DockerDesktop.exe scheduled-task/Defender-exclusion UC, review Bing/ad-referred downloads across the fleet, and check for SectopRAT credit-card/credential exfil beacons.
let ClaudeLure = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ClaudeDesktop.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="ClaudeDesktop.exe execution", Path=FolderPath, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let LibcefSideload = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "libcef.dll"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="libcef.dll side-load from staging dir", Path=FolderPath, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256=InitiatingProcessSHA256;
union ClaudeLure, LibcefSideload
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ClaudeDesktop.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeAgent SectopRAT persistence: DockerDesktop.exe scheduled task + Defender exclusion AIInstallation High
Hunts the FakeAgent post-exploitation persistence — a dropped DockerDesktop.exe registered as a scheduled task, plus Add-MpPreference Defender exclusions the operator sets to protect the payload. Both are hardcoded behaviours Huntress observed across the 29 victim organizations. Rationale: DockerDesktop.exe as a scheduled-task persistence binary (genuine Docker Desktop ships as 'Docker Desktop.exe' with a space, in Program Files) plus Add-MpPreference exclusions are the two persistence/evasion steps Huntress documented for FakeAgent; both are user-context, non-machine-account actions. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/23/fakeagent-campaign-malicious-claude-artifact-used-to-distribute-sectoprat-to-29-organisations/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Docker Desktop install task ('Docker Desktop.exe' with space, under Program Files) — the no-space DockerDesktop.exe token reduces overlap
  • Endpoint/AV admin legitimately adding a Defender exclusion via Add-MpPreference during troubleshooting
  • EDR or software-deployment tooling registering scheduled tasks under SYSTEM (filtered by machine-account exclusion)
  • A developer scripting Register-ScheduledTask for a personal automation named 'Docker...'
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has @"\Program Files\Docker\Docker\Docker Desktop.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the scheduled-task action path/hash for DockerDesktop.exe (confirm it's in a user-writable dir, not Program Files) and enumerate any Defender exclusions added around the same time (Get-MpPreference) to see what the operator is protecting. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the rogue task, remove the exclusion, and quarantine DockerDesktop.exe and the associated ClaudeDesktop.exe/libcef.dll bundle. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same DockerDesktop.exe task name and identical exclusion paths, and correlate to the FakeAgent delivery UC (ClaudeDesktop.exe / libcef.dll side-load).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("/create","DockerDesktop.exe"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("Register-ScheduledTask","DockerDesktop"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-ExclusionPath","-ExclusionProcess"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "DockerDesktop.exe")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and CommandLine has_any ("-ExclusionPath","-ExclusionProcess"))
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask" and CommandLine has "DockerDesktop")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FakeAgent SectopRAT persistence via DockerDesktop.exe task or Defender exclusion
id: c81f5a67-2b90-4e13-8d6c-9f0a4b7e5d22
description: Detects the FakeAgent campaign persistence steps - registering a dropped DockerDesktop.exe as a scheduled task or adding a Microsoft Defender exclusion via Add-MpPreference
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-android-spyware-plc-attacks.html
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/fakeagent-claude-desktop-malvertising-ends-in-dotnet-rat
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  sel_task:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/create'
      - 'DockerDesktop.exe'
  sel_defender:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'Add-MpPreference'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-ExclusionPath'
      - '-ExclusionProcess'
  condition: sel_task or sel_defender
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*DockerDesktop.exe* AND */create*)) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:*Add-MpPreference* AND @CommandLine:(*-ExclusionPath* OR *-ExclusionProcess*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\/create/i CommandLine=/DockerDesktop\.exe/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/Add-MpPreference/i CommandLine=/(ExclusionPath|ExclusionProcess)/i)
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*DockerDesktop.exe*" AND Processes.process="*/create*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Add-MpPreference*" AND Processes.process="*Exclusion*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*DockerDesktop.exe*" AND Processes.process="*/create*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Add-MpPreference*" AND Processes.process="*Exclusion*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium

Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain

ImDnsActivity

            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"

| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing from campaign sender 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain malware chain) · [LLM] ClickUp-hosted Financial_report.bat dropper written to disk · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Batch dropper spawns hidden PowerShell pulling installer.exe from pixeldrain.com · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint network/DNS egress to pixeldrain.com from a LOLBin / script host · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound phishing from campaign sender 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain malware chain) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail from the DKIM-signed campaign sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com / Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com that Microsoft attributed to the June 2026 multi-stage chain delivering a nested Teams-voicemail EML lure. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact sender IOCs rather than generic phishing heuristics. Rationale: Anchors on the exact table-1 IOCs (9i6pokerdepot.com sender domain and Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com address) Microsoft published for the June 2026 chain; a fixed malicious sender domain is a low-FP alerting anchor. Enriched with EmailAttachmentInfo to surface the nested EML lure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team replaying the sample phish into a test mailbox for detection tuning
  • Threat-intel platform detonating the sample and generating internal mail with the sender string
  • Purple-team exercise reusing the IOC domain in a simulation
  • A benign look-alike domain if the operator's registration lapses and someone else re-registers 9i6pokerdepot.com
Suppression filter
| where RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("phishtest@yourorg.com","soc-detonation@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm EmailDirection is Inbound and DeliveryAction=Delivered; pull recipients and check whether any opened the nested EML / clicked the "Listen to Voicemail" button via UrlClickEvents. Step 2 (contain): Soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com, and quarantine any clickup-attachments.com or pixeldrain.com URLs. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot recipients to UC-3/UC-4 to check for Financial_report.bat execution or pixeldrain.com egress on their devices in the following 24h.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailAttachmentInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | project NetworkMessageId, AttFile = FileName, FileType) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttFile, FileType, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailAttachmentInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | project NetworkMessageId, AttFile = FileName, FileType) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttFile, FileType, AuthenticationDetails

ClickUp-hosted Financial_report.bat dropper written to disk AIDelivery High
Detects the stage-2 Windows batch dropper (Financial_report.bat) being downloaded from ClickUp's public attachment host t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com. Article-specific: a .bat file originating from clickup-attachments.com is the exact abuse Microsoft documented, distinct from legitimate ClickUp document sharing. Rationale: Uses the exact stage-2 artifacts Microsoft/second-source reporting confirmed: the clickup-attachments.com origin host (table 1) and the Financial_report.bat filename. A batch file whose FileOriginUrl is clickup-attachments.com is a high-fidelity, low-volume anchor; downstream queries fall back to the specific filename where download-origin telemetry is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163
ATT&CKT1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately downloading a build/automation .bat shared via a corporate ClickUp workspace
  • IT distributing a maintenance batch script through ClickUp attachments
  • Analyst re-downloading the sample to a sandbox for analysis
  • Unrelated file literally named Financial_report.bat created by a finance automation tool
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm FileOriginUrl points to clickup-attachments.com and identify the writing process (browser vs. mail client) and the user. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host if the .bat has executed (check UC-3), delete/quarantine the dropper, and block clickup-attachments.com download paths at the proxy for non-business ClickUp use. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host for powershell.exe spawned by cmd.exe running the .bat and for installer.exe in %TEMP% and pixeldrain.com egress (UC-3/UC-4).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileOriginUrl has "clickup-attachments.com" and FileName endswith ".bat")
    or FileName =~ "Financial_report.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "clickup-attachments.com"
| where Url has ".bat" or FileName endswith ".bat"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, FileName, FileMimeType, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Batch dropper spawns hidden PowerShell pulling installer.exe from pixeldrain.com AIInstallation High
Detects the execution stage: cmd/batch spawning a hidden PowerShell that downloads installer.exe from pixeldrain.com into %TEMP%, runs it silently, then self-deletes. Article-specific because pixeldrain.com in a script command line is the exact final-payload retrieval host Microsoft published. Rationale: pixeldrain.com in a scripting-host command line is the exact final-installer retrieval Microsoft and the second-source write-up documented; it is rare enough in enterprise scripting to alert on directly, and the cmd->hidden-powershell->pixeldrain->self-delete chain matches the published behavior precisely. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1564.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or researcher legitimately using curl/PowerShell to fetch a file shared via pixeldrain.com
  • Security analyst manually reproducing the download in an isolated VM
  • A CI/automation script pulling an artifact from a pixeldrain link
  • Rare power-user using pixeldrain as personal file transfer over corporate device
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the full command line and parent process — confirm parent is cmd.exe running a .bat and the child is hidden-window PowerShell/curl; check for installer.exe written to the user's Temp. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the process tree, capture installer.exe (or its FileWritten hash before self-delete) for analysis, and block pixeldrain.com egress. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the fleet for the same pixeldrain.com command-line pattern and for the delivery IOCs (UC-1 sender, UC-2 clickup .bat) to scope other recipients who executed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pixeldrain.com"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| extend HiddenOrTemp = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","hidden","-nop","-noprofile","\\Temp\\","installer.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HiddenOrTemp, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "pixeldrain.com"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Script host downloading installer.exe from pixeldrain.com
id: c19a7e30-4b6d-4c22-8f7e-1a2b3c4d5e6f
description: Detects powershell/cmd/curl referencing pixeldrain.com in the command line, matching the Q2 2026 Microsoft-documented final-payload retrieval (installer.exe to %TEMP%, silent run, dropper self-delete).
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1564.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'pixeldrain.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*pixeldrain.com* @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/pixeldrain\.com/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*pixeldrain.com*" AND (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="curl.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*pixeldrain.com*" AND (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="curl.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Endpoint network/DNS egress to pixeldrain.com from a LOLBin / script host AICommand & Control Medium
Network-telemetry safety-net for the final payload retrieval: any host resolving/connecting to pixeldrain.com, especially initiated by a scripting host or LOLBin rather than a browser. Catches the download even when command-line auditing is disabled and the dropper name varies. Rationale: pixeldrain.com is the named final-payload host (table 1 URL hxxps://pixeldrain[.]com/api/file/3v92oJiL) and is uncommon in corporate traffic; scoping the initiator to LOLBins/script hosts keeps it high-signal while surviving cases where command-line logging (UC-3) is off. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://any.run/report/84f73741867e012140103aa9eb59bfaef6bf8c02aa7b9579be7aad2143418c03/18abf34d-1f07-4902-8343-13b9f8358605
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately downloading a file someone shared via pixeldrain in a browser (excluded by the LOLBin initiator filter in Defender, but DNS-only sources will still see it)
  • Researcher/sandbox pulling samples from pixeldrain
  • Security tooling enriching pixeldrain IOCs by resolving the domain
  • curl/PowerShell used by a developer to fetch a legitimately shared artifact
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process — a browser is likely benign, but powershell/cmd/curl/certutil to pixeldrain is high-priority; correlate with any installer.exe write in %TEMP% on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host if a script host initiated the connection, block pixeldrain.com at the egress proxy/DNS, and collect the downloaded binary. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the host and user back to UC-1 (campaign email) and UC-2 (clickup .bat) to confirm the full chain and identify other victims resolving pixeldrain.com in the same window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "pixeldrain.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "pixeldrain.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS resolution of pixeldrain.com file-hosting domain
id: e5d8b271-3a49-4f10-9c62-7d81ab34ce90
description: Detects DNS queries for pixeldrain.com, the final installer host in the Q2 2026 Microsoft-documented ClickUp/pixeldrain malware chain. Rare in enterprise; tune to script-host initiators.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains: 'pixeldrain.com'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:*pixeldrain.com* @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/pixeldrain\.com/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*pixeldrain.com*" by DNS.src, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*pixeldrain.com*" by DNS.src, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Auth.js v5 fail-open trigger: server-configuration error emitted in app logs AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact Auth.js/next-auth v5 configuration-error log lines (InvalidEndpoints, MissingSecret/AUTH_SECRET, or the generic 'problem with the server configuration' message) that flip the auth() wrapper into returning a truthy error object instead of null. Once this appears, any middleware using existence-only checks (!!auth / if(req.auth)) fails open and treats every request as authenticated. Rationale: Uses the advisory's verbatim strings: the '[auth][error]' prefix, the named error classes 'InvalidEndpoints' and 'MissingSecret'/'AUTH_SECRET', and the surfaced message 'problem with the server configuration'. These are high-fidelity because they are Auth.js internal error identifiers that appear only when the configuration breaks — the precise precondition for the fail-open state. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Transient config error during a rolling deploy that is corrected within seconds (env var briefly unset)
  • Non-production/staging hosts intentionally running with an incomplete provider config
  • A monitoring or documentation tool echoing the error text back into logs
  • Local developer environment logs shipped to the same index
  • Deliberate chaos/DR testing of the auth layer
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "dev" and HostName !has "preview"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the app is on a vulnerable next-auth build (>=5.0.0-beta.0, <=5.0.0-beta.31) and that middleware uses existence-only checks (!!auth / if(req.auth)) rather than !!req.auth?.user; identify the affected host/environment and whether it is internet-facing. 2) CONTAIN: Restore the missing env var (AUTH_SECRET / provider issuer|authorization) or roll back the deploy; if it is production and internet-facing, gate traffic at the LB until fixed and apply the documented workaround (check req.auth?.user). 3) HUNT: Pull access logs for the error window and look for successful (200/302) requests to protected routes from sessions with no auth cookie — pivot to UC 'Auth.js fail-open: protected-route access during a config-error window'.
// Auth.js config-error state that causes existence-based auth checks to fail open
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("InvalidEndpoints", "MissingSecret", "AUTH_SECRET", "problem with the server configuration")
| summarize ErrorCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleLog = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Auth.js v5 Fail-Open Configuration Error (InvalidEndpoints / MissingSecret)
id: a4dbb25b-f4c7-5bdd-af42-49468d365b01
description: Detects Auth.js (next-auth v5) server-configuration errors that cause the auth() wrapper to return a truthy error object, making existence-based auth checks fail open (GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3
  - https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  product: nodejs
  service: application
detection:
  selection_prefix:
    keywords:
      - '[auth][error]'
  selection_error:
    keywords:
      - 'InvalidEndpoints'
      - 'MissingSecret'
      - 'AUTH_SECRET'
      - 'problem with the server configuration'
  condition: selection_prefix and selection_error
level: high
"[auth][error]" AND ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET" OR "problem with the server configuration")
# log group: /aws/lambda/<your-nextjs-app>  (or the ECS/app-runner app log group hosting Auth.js)
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @message like /\[auth\]\[error\]/ and @message like /(InvalidEndpoints|MissingSecret|AUTH_SECRET|problem with the server configuration)/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200
APPLICATION
index=* ("[auth][error]") ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET" OR "problem with the server configuration")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sampleLog by host, source, sourcetype
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Auth.js fail-open: protected-route access succeeds during a config-error window AIExploitation Medium
Correlates Auth.js '[auth][error]' log lines with successful (200/302) HTTP responses to protected application routes in the same short time window. During the config-error state the auth object is truthy for everyone, so unauthenticated requests to gated routes start returning success instead of redirect/401 — this catches the bypass being exercised, not just the enabling condition. Rationale: Ties the advisory's cause ('[auth][error]' -> truthy auth object) to its observable effect (protected routes returning 200/302 to requests that should have been denied). Scoping to /api/ excluding /api/auth targets application-protected routes without a customer-specific placeholder; the AnonReqs/empty-username count highlights sessions that succeeded without an authenticated user. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1556 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuinely public /api routes that are intentionally unauthenticated (health, webhooks, public content)
  • Config error and legitimate authenticated traffic simply coinciding in the same 5-minute bin
  • API routes that perform their own token/role check downstream and are not gated by the vulnerable middleware
  • Load-balancer or uptime-probe hitting API endpoints during the error window
  • Static/cached responses served without hitting the auth middleware
Suppression filter
| where not(CsUriStem in ("/api/health", "/api/healthz", "/api/ping", "/api/webhooks"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged bin, pull the individual AppServiceHTTPLogs rows and check whether the succeeding requests carried a valid session cookie / CsUsername — no-cookie 200s to a gated route during an error window are true positives. 2) CONTAIN: Fix the underlying config (restore AUTH_SECRET / provider endpoints) or roll back; treat any data returned to unauthenticated callers as potentially exposed and revoke/rotate as needed. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every distinct source IP and path served during the window, and search for follow-on actions (data reads, privileged API calls) from those IPs after the fail-open period.
// Successful protected-route access occurring in the same 5-min bin as an Auth.js config error = fail-open exercised
let ErrBins = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | extend Bin = bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
    | distinct Bin;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/" and not(CsUriStem startswith "/api/auth")
| extend Bin = bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| join kind=inner (ErrBins) on Bin
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(CIp, 50), AnonReqs = countif(isempty(CsUsername)) by Bin, CsHost
| order by Bin desc
CLOUD

| rename Web.* as *
| join type=inner _time [
    search index=* "[auth][error]"
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count as authErrors by _time ]
| where authErrors > 0
| stats sum(count) as okProtectedReqs values(url) as urls values(src) as sourceIPs by _time, site

Auth.js: protected /api access returning success with no session cookie (fail-open evidence) AIExploitation Medium
Standalone hunt for the observable outcome of the bypass: successful (200/302) responses to protected application routes where the request carried NO Auth.js session cookie (authjs.session-token / __Secure-authjs.session-token). Under the vulnerable existence-only check, an unauthenticated request with no session cookie is granted access — this surfaces that outcome even without pairing to the error log. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's core claim that access is granted to 'every request, including unauthenticated ones', combined with the known Auth.js v5 default session-cookie name 'authjs.session-token' (and its '__Secure-' HTTPS variant). A gated /api route returning 200/302 to a request with no session cookie and no authenticated user is the direct fingerprint of the fail-open. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately public /api endpoints that never require a session (health, public config, webhooks)
  • First request of a login flow before any session cookie is set
  • API keys / bearer-token auth used instead of session cookies (auth carried in Authorization header, not the cookie)
  • Access logs that do not capture the Cookie header, causing every row to look cookie-less
  • CDN/edge-cached API responses served without the origin auth middleware
Suppression filter
| where not(CsUriStem in ("/api/health", "/api/healthz", "/api/ping", "/api/webhooks", "/api/public"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the flagged /api paths are actually meant to be authenticated (not public); check whether auth is expected via Authorization header rather than cookie before calling it a bypass. 2) CONTAIN: If confirmed, apply the Auth.js fix/workaround (check req.auth?.user, restore config) and revoke exposure; block the offending source IPs if abuse is evident. 3) HUNT: Cross-reference these no-cookie successes against '[auth][error]' log windows to confirm causation, and review what data/actions those requests obtained to scope the exposure.
// Protected /api routes returning success to a request that carried NO Auth.js session cookie
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/" and not(CsUriStem startswith "/api/auth")
| where isempty(Cookie) or Cookie !contains "authjs.session-token"
| where isempty(CsUsername)
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CsHost, CIp
| where Requests > 0
| order by LastSeen desc
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype=*:access* (status=200 OR status=302) uri_path="/api/*" NOT uri_path="/api/auth*" NOT cookie="*authjs.session-token*"
| stats count as reqs values(uri_path) as paths dc(src_ip) as srcIPs by host, src_ip
| where reqs > 0
| sort - reqs

1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (browser vs. service); confirm the user has an active Zimbra webmail session and whether the org runs unpatched ZCS (<10.0.18 / <10.1.13). 2) Contain: block all nine domains/IPs at proxy+DNS, isolate the host, and force-reset the affected user's Zimbra password and 2FA scratch codes (the payload steals both). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/device for the last 90 days of mailbox access, search all endpoints for any of the nine IOCs, and review Zimbra logs for the CSS @import XSS mail that triggered it.
